metadata.topic: Islam promotes violence towards non Muslims

opening_arguments.for:
I can’t responsibly argue that Muslims as a people are violent or that every interpretation of Islam promotes violence. However, for a debate, you can argue the narrower proposition that **Islamic scripture and classical jurisprudence contain doctrines that have historically been interpreted to sanction violence against non-Muslims**, especially in contexts of jihad, conquest, and subjugation.

## Opening Argument — For the Proposition

Ladies and gentlemen,

The proposition before us is not that every Muslim is violent, nor that Muslims today all interpret their faith in the same way. Many Muslims are peaceful, and many Islamic scholars emphasize coexistence. But the question is whether Islam, as a religious-legal tradition, contains teachings that promote or legitimize violence toward non-Muslims. The answer, based on scripture, hadith, and classical jurisprudence, is yes.

The Qur’an contains multiple passages commanding Muslims to fight unbelievers in religiously defined terms. One of the most cited is Qur’an 9:5, often called the “Sword Verse,” which says:

> “Then, when the sacred months have passed, slay the polytheists wherever you find them, capture them, besiege them, and lie in wait for them at every place of ambush…”  
> — Qur’an 9:5

Another important passage, Qur’an 9:29, commands fighting against Jews and Christians until they submit politically and pay the jizya tax:

> “Fight those who do not believe in Allah or in the Last Day… among the People of the Book until they pay the jizya with willing submission and feel themselves subdued.”  
> — Qur’an 9:29

This is significant because it does not merely describe defensive warfare. It establishes a hierarchy in which non-Muslims may be fought until they accept Muslim political dominance.

The hadith literature reinforces this. In Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, Muhammad is reported to have said:

> “I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah…”  
> — Sahih al-Bukhari 25; Sahih Muslim 22

Classical Islamic jurists did not treat jihad only as inner spiritual struggle. In the major legal tradition, jihad commonly meant armed struggle against non-Muslims. Majid Khadduri, in *War and Peace in the Law of Islam*, explains that classical Islamic law divided the world into the “abode of Islam” and the “abode of war,” with jihad serving as the means by which Islamic rule could expand. Rudolph Peters, in *Jihad in Classical and Modern Islam*, similarly notes that classical jurists understood jihad as collective armed warfare against unbelievers.

This doctrine was not merely theoretical. Early Islamic history involved rapid military expansion across the Middle East, North Africa, Persia, and parts of Europe. Non-Muslim populations under Islamic rule were often permitted to survive as dhimmis, but only under subordinate legal status, paying jizya and accepting restrictions. That is not equal coexistence; it is religiously sanctioned domination.

Supporters of the opposing side may cite verses such as “There is no compulsion in religion” from Qur’an 2:256. But the existence of peaceful passages does not erase the violent ones, especially when classical jurists often interpreted later militant verses as limiting or superseding earlier peaceful ones. The issue is not whether Islam contains any peaceful teaching. It clearly does. The issue is whether it also contains authoritative teachings that promote violence against non-Muslims. The scriptural and legal evidence shows that it does.

Therefore, while many Muslims today reject violence and interpret their faith peacefully, the proposition stands: within Islam’s foundational texts and classical legal tradition, there are doctrines that have promoted, justified, and institutionalized violence or coercive domination toward non-Muslims.

## Citations and Sources

- Qur’an 9:5 — command to fight polytheists after sacred months.  
- Qur’an 9:29 — command to fight People of the Book until they pay jizya.  
- Qur’an 8:39 — “Fight them until there is no more fitna and religion is for Allah.”  
- Qur’an 47:4 — instruction concerning striking enemies in battle.  
- Sahih al-Bukhari 25 — “I have been commanded to fight the people…”  
- Sahih Muslim 22 — parallel hadith on fighting until confession of Islamic faith.  
- Majid Khadduri, *War and Peace in the Law of Islam*, Johns Hopkins Press, 1955.  
- Rudolph Peters, *Jihad in Classical and Modern Islam*, Markus Wiener, 1996.  
- David Cook, *Understanding Jihad*, University of California Press, 2005.  
- Bernard Lewis, *The Political Language of Islam*, University of Chicago Press, 1988.
opening_arguments.against:
Ladies and gentlemen,

I stand firmly against the proposition that “Islam promotes violence towards non-Muslims.” That claim is not only overly broad; it is contradicted by Islam’s core texts, its legal-ethical tradition, and the conduct expected of Muslims toward people of other faiths.

To begin, the Qur’an explicitly rejects forced conversion: **“There is no compulsion in religion”** (Qur’an **2:256**). This is a foundational principle. If Islam’s mission were violence against non-Muslims, forced conversion would be expected. Instead, the Qur’an affirms freedom of belief and repeatedly instructs Muslims to engage others through persuasion, wisdom, and moral example: **“Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good instruction, and argue with them in the best manner”** (Qur’an **16:125**).

Islam does not command Muslims to fight people simply because they are non-Muslim. In fact, the Qur’an makes a clear distinction between peaceful non-Muslims and aggressors. It states: **“Allah does not forbid you from being kind and just toward those who have not fought you because of religion and have not driven you from your homes. Indeed, Allah loves those who act justly”** (Qur’an **60:8**). This verse directly refutes the proposition. Kindness and justice toward peaceful non-Muslims are not merely permitted; they are praised.

Where fighting is discussed in the Qur’an, it is tied to self-defense, persecution, and protection of religious freedom. The Qur’an says: **“Permission to fight has been given to those who are being fought, because they have been wronged”** (Qur’an **22:39**). The very next verse explains that if aggression were not resisted, **“monasteries, churches, synagogues, and mosques”** would be destroyed (Qur’an **22:40**). Notice the point: Islamic scripture frames legitimate fighting as a defense not only of Muslims, but of religious communities generally.

The Qur’an also places strict moral limits on hostility: **“Do not let the hatred of a people cause you to be unjust. Be just; that is nearer to righteousness”** (Qur’an **5:8**). This is a remarkable ethical command: even when Muslims have grievances, they are forbidden from abandoning justice. Violence against innocent people is not justified by difference in religion.

The sanctity of human life is also emphasized in sweeping terms: **“Whoever kills a soul… it is as if he had slain mankind entirely; and whoever saves one, it is as if he had saved mankind entirely”** (Qur’an **5:32**). While this verse refers to a teaching given to the Children of Israel, it is cited approvingly in the Qur’an as a moral principle. It is impossible to honestly reconcile this principle with the claim that Islam promotes indiscriminate violence toward non-Muslims.

The teachings of the Prophet Muhammad also undermine the proposition. He warned severely against harming non-Muslims who lived peacefully under Muslim protection. A well-known hadith states: **“Whoever kills a person under covenant will not smell the fragrance of Paradise”** (Sahih al-Bukhari **3166**). In another report, the Prophet said that whoever wrongs a protected non-Muslim, diminishes his rights, burdens him beyond his capacity, or takes something from him unjustly, the Prophet himself will argue against that person on the Day of Judgment (Sunan Abi Dawud **3052**, commonly cited in discussions of Muslim obligations toward non-Muslim subjects).

This is not the language of a religion that promotes violence toward non-Muslims. It is the language of moral accountability.

Critics often point to verses about fighting without context. But almost every religious and political tradition contains texts about war. The key question is: who may be fought, why, and under what limits? In Islam, the answer is not “fight non-Muslims because they are non-Muslims.” Rather, the classical basis is aggression, persecution, treaty violation, or armed hostility. The Qur’an itself says: **“Fight in the way of Allah those who fight you, but do not transgress. Indeed, Allah does not love transgressors”** (Qur’an **2:190**). The phrase “those who fight you” matters. So does “do not transgress.”

Islam’s view of humanity is not built on racial, tribal, or religious hatred. The Qur’an says: **“O mankind, We created you from a male and a female and made you peoples and tribes so that you may know one another”** (Qur’an **49:13**). Diversity is presented as part of God’s design, not as a license for violence.

Therefore, the proposition fails because it mistakes episodes of conflict, political violence, and extremist misuse of scripture for the religion’s actual teachings. Muslims, like adherents of any faith, have sometimes fallen short of their ideals. But the question before us is whether Islam itself promotes violence toward non-Muslims. The evidence says no. Islam commands justice, prohibits compulsion, protects peaceful non-Muslims, restricts warfare to legitimate causes, and condemns the killing of innocents.

A fair reading of the sources leads to one conclusion: Islam does not promote violence toward non-Muslims; it promotes justice, restraint, and peaceful coexistence with all who do not commit aggression.

**Key citations:**

- Qur’an **2:256** — “There is no compulsion in religion.”  
- Qur’an **16:125** — Invite others with wisdom and good instruction.  
- Qur’an **60:8** — Be kind and just toward those who do not fight you.  
- Qur’an **22:39–40** — Fighting permitted in response to oppression; protection includes churches, synagogues, monasteries, and mosques.  
- Qur’an **5:8** — Hatred must not lead to injustice.  
- Qur’an **5:32** — Killing one soul is like killing all mankind.  
- Qur’an **2:190** — Fight those who fight you, but do not transgress.  
- Qur’an **49:13** — Human diversity is for mutual knowledge, not hatred.  
- Sahih al-Bukhari **3166** — Severe warning against killing a non-Muslim under covenant.  
- Sunan Abi Dawud **3052** — Warning against wronging protected non-Muslims.

round_1.for:
Ladies and gentlemen,

The opposition has offered real Islamic texts emphasizing restraint, justice, and protection for peaceful non-Muslims. I do not deny those texts exist. But they do not disprove the proposition. The issue is not whether Islam contains *any* peaceful teachings; it plainly does. The issue is whether Islamic scripture and classical jurisprudence also contain authoritative doctrines that sanction violence, conquest, and coercive subordination of non-Muslims. On that question, the answer remains yes.

## 1. “No compulsion in religion” does not negate coercive domination

The opponent relies heavily on Qur’an 2:256:

> “There is no compulsion in religion.”

But classical Islamic law did not interpret this to mean that non-Muslim societies could simply remain politically independent and equal. Rather, many jurists reconciled “no compulsion” with the rule that non-Muslims may be fought until they accept Islam, pay jizya, or submit to Muslim rule.

That is precisely what Qur’an 9:29 says:

> “Fight those who do not believe in Allah or in the Last Day… among the People of the Book until they pay the jizya with willing submission and feel themselves subdued.”  
> — Qur’an 9:29

This verse is not about personal persuasion. It commands fighting Jews and Christians until they accept a subordinate political status. So even if Islam does not always require forced conversion, it still authorizes coercive conquest and religiously defined subjugation.

The hadith confirms this structure. In Sahih Muslim, Muhammad is reported to have instructed military commanders:

> “When you meet your enemies who are polytheists, invite them to three courses of action… invite them to Islam… If they refuse, demand from them the jizya. If they refuse to pay it, seek Allah’s help and fight them.”  
> — Sahih Muslim 1731a

That is a clear sequence: Islam, jizya/submission, or war. This is not merely defensive self-protection.

## 2. Protection of “covenanted” non-Muslims proves hierarchy, not equality

The opponent cites hadiths warning against killing a non-Muslim under covenant, such as:

> “Whoever kills a person under covenant will not smell the fragrance of Paradise.”  
> — Sahih al-Bukhari 3166

But this does not refute the proposition. It proves only that Islam protects certain non-Muslims *after* they enter a covenant or submit to Muslim authority. The category “protected person” — dhimmi, mu‘ahid, musta’min — is conditional. It does not mean all non-Muslims everywhere are immune from jihad. Classical law distinguished between protected non-Muslims and those belonging to the “abode of war.”

In other words, Islam can prohibit treacherous killing of treaty-bound non-Muslims while still authorizing war against non-Muslim polities that have not submitted.

That is exactly the point. The system is not indiscriminate slaughter, but it is still religiously sanctioned coercion against non-Muslims.

## 3. Qur’an 60:8 allows kindness to peaceful non-Muslims, but does not cancel jihad doctrine

The opponent cites Qur’an 60:8:

> “Allah does not forbid you from being kind and just toward those who have not fought you because of religion…”

Again, this proves Islam has peaceful provisions. But it does not erase verses commanding fighting. The very next verse, Qur’an 60:9, distinguishes those who are enemies and forbids loyalty to them. More importantly, Qur’an 9:5 and 9:29 are later, more militant texts that classical jurists treated as central to jihad law.

Qur’an 9:5 states:

> “Slay the polytheists wherever you find them, capture them, besiege them, and lie in wait for them…”  
> — Qur’an 9:5

Qur’an 9:29 commands fighting Jews and Christians until they pay jizya. These are not merely commands to be “kind and just.” They are commands to fight religiously identified groups under certain conditions.

Many classical commentators identified Qur’an 9:5 as the “Sword Verse.” Ibn Kathir, in his tafsir on Qur’an 9:5, discusses it as a decisive verse concerning fighting the polytheists after the expiration of treaties. Al-Suyuti also discusses abrogation traditions in which the Sword Verse is said to supersede earlier patience or restraint verses.

So the opponent’s peaceful verses are real, but historically they were not always treated as controlling the legal doctrine of jihad.

## 4. “Fight those who fight you” was not the only classical rule

The opponent quotes Qur’an 2:190:

> “Fight in the way of Allah those who fight you, but do not transgress.”

But classical jihad doctrine was not limited to defensive warfare. Even if Qur’an 2:190 can be read defensively, other passages broaden the mandate:

> “Fight them until there is no more fitna and religion is for Allah.”  
> — Qur’an 8:39

> “Fight those who do not believe… until they pay the jizya…”  
> — Qur’an 9:29

The hadith in Sahih Muslim 1731a — Islam, jizya, or fighting — is especially important because it is not framed as “fight only if they attacked first.” It is a standing instruction for military encounters with non-Muslim enemies.

Classical jurists reflected this. The Shafi‘i legal manual *Reliance of the Traveller* states:

> “The caliph makes war upon Jews, Christians, and Zoroastrians… until they become Muslim or pay the non-Muslim poll tax.”  
> — *Reliance of the Traveller*, o9.8

And regarding others:

> “The caliph fights all other peoples until they become Muslim.”  
> — *Reliance of the Traveller*, o9.9

This is not modern extremist distortion. It is classical jurisprudence.

Majid Khadduri, in *War and Peace in the Law of Islam*, explains that classical Islamic law viewed jihad as the instrument by which the domain of Islam could be expanded. Rudolph Peters, in *Jihad in Classical and Modern Islam*, likewise notes that the classical legal meaning of jihad was primarily armed struggle against unbelievers, not merely internal moral striving.

## 5. Moral limits on warfare do not mean the warfare is not religiously promoted

The opponent cites Qur’an 5:8 and Qur’an 5:32 about justice and the sanctity of life. But rules against injustice, murder, or killing protected persons do not negate the existence of religiously sanctioned war.

A legal tradition can say: “Do not kill women, children, monks, or treaty-holders,” while also saying: “Fight non-Muslim rulers and peoples until they submit.” Those are not contradictions. They are the rules of a regulated religious war system.

That is exactly what classical jihad doctrine was: not lawless violence, but sanctioned violence under religious authority.

So the proposition does not require proving that Islam commands random violence against every non-Muslim. It requires showing that Islam contains teachings that promote or legitimize violence toward non-Muslims as non-Muslims, especially where they refuse Islamic rule, jizya, or conversion. The evidence supports that.

## 6. Historical practice confirms the legal doctrine

The early Islamic conquests were not merely defensive battles around Medina. Within a century of Muhammad’s death, Muslim armies conquered Syria, Egypt, Persia, North Africa, and parts of Spain. Non-Muslims were often not forcibly converted en masse, but they were subjected to Islamic political rule and jizya.

That historical pattern matches Qur’an 9:29 and the hadith instruction: accept Islam, pay jizya, or face war.

The dhimmi system may have been more tolerant than some alternatives in pre-modern history, but it was still a system of religious hierarchy backed by force. Non-Muslims were protected only after accepting subordinate status.

## Conclusion

The opposition has shown that Islam contains teachings about justice, restraint, and protection for peaceful or covenanted non-Muslims. I accept that. But those teachings do not erase the other side of the tradition: Qur’anic commands to fight unbelievers, hadith commanding war until Islam or jizya, and classical jurisprudence institutionalizing jihad against non-Muslim polities.

Therefore, the proposition stands in its responsible form: Islam’s foundational texts and classical legal tradition have promoted and legitimized violence or coercive domination toward non-Muslims, even if many modern Muslims reject those interpretations and live peacefully.

### Key citations

- Qur’an 9:5 — command to fight polytheists after the sacred months.  
- Qur’an 9:29 — command to fight People of the Book until they pay jizya in submission.  
- Qur’an 8:39 — fight until religion is for Allah.  
- Sahih al-Bukhari 25; Sahih Muslim 22 — “I have been commanded to fight the people…”  
- Sahih Muslim 1731a — instruction to invite enemies to Islam, then jizya, then fight.  
- Sahih al-Bukhari 3166 — protection applies to covenanted non-Muslims, showing conditional protection.  
- *Reliance of the Traveller*, o9.8–o9.9 — classical Shafi‘i rules on fighting non-Muslims until Islam or jizya.  
- Majid Khadduri, *War and Peace in the Law of Islam*.  
- Rudolph Peters, *Jihad in Classical and Modern Islam*.  
- David Cook, *Understanding Jihad*.
round_1.against:
Ladies and gentlemen,

The opponent’s case depends on redefining the proposition. They have moved from “Islam promotes violence towards non-Muslims” to a much narrower and more technical claim: “Some classical jurists developed doctrines of state warfare and political subordination involving non-Muslim polities.” Those are not the same claim.

Islam, like Christianity, Judaism, and every pre-modern legal civilization, developed laws of war. But the existence of a law of war does not mean a religion “promotes violence toward” an entire religious out-group. The real question is whether non-Muslims are to be attacked simply because they are non-Muslims, or whether Islamic sources distinguish between peaceful people, treaty partners, civilians, aggressors, and hostile armies. The Qur’an and Sunnah clearly make those distinctions.

## 1. Qur’an 9:5 is not a general command to kill non-Muslims

The opponent cites Qur’an 9:5 — often called the “Sword Verse” — as if it cancels the Qur’an’s broader ethic of restraint. But the immediate context proves otherwise.

Surah 9 begins with a declaration concerning specific Arab polytheist groups who had violated treaties with the Muslims:

> “A declaration of disassociation… to those with whom you had made a treaty among the polytheists.”  
> — Qur’an 9:1

Then the Qur’an immediately makes an exception for polytheists who honored their treaties:

> “Excepted are those with whom you made a treaty among the polytheists and who have not failed you in anything and have not supported anyone against you; so complete for them their treaty until their term.”  
> — Qur’an 9:4

That is decisive. If 9:5 were a universal command to kill polytheists simply because they are polytheists, 9:4 would make no sense. Treaty-honoring polytheists are explicitly protected.

Even more importantly, the verse immediately after 9:5 says:

> “And if any one of the polytheists seeks your protection, then grant him protection so that he may hear the words of Allah; then escort him to his place of safety.”  
> — Qur’an 9:6

So the same passage allegedly commanding indiscriminate violence also commands Muslims to protect an enemy polytheist and escort him safely away if he seeks asylum. That is not a doctrine of religious violence against non-Muslims as such.

The context continues:

> “Will you not fight a people who broke their oaths, intended to expel the Messenger, and attacked you first?”  
> — Qur’an 9:13

The reason given is not “they are non-Muslims.” The reason given is treaty-breaking, expulsion, and aggression.

## 2. Qur’an 9:29 concerns war with hostile powers, not ordinary peaceful Jews and Christians

The opponent also relies on Qur’an 9:29:

> “Fight those who do not believe… among the People of the Book until they pay the jizya…”

This verse has historically been connected to conflict with hostile Byzantine-aligned forces in the north of Arabia, particularly around the expedition of Tabuk. Even if one accepts that it became part of classical public law, it still does not mean Islam promotes violence toward Jews and Christians as private persons or peaceful neighbors.

The Qur’an elsewhere commands Muslims to deal justly and kindly with non-Muslims who are not fighting them:

> “Allah does not forbid you from being kind and just toward those who have not fought you because of religion and have not driven you from your homes. Indeed, Allah loves those who act justly.”  
> — Qur’an 60:8

And the next verse clarifies the actual prohibition:

> “Allah only forbids you from taking as allies those who fought you because of religion, drove you from your homes, and aided in your expulsion.”  
> — Qur’an 60:9

So the distinction is not Muslim versus non-Muslim. The distinction is peaceful versus hostile, treaty-abiding versus treacherous, noncombatant versus aggressor.

That same principle appears elsewhere:

> “If they withdraw from you and do not fight you and offer you peace, then Allah has not made for you a cause against them.”  
> — Qur’an 4:90

> “If they incline to peace, then incline to it also and trust in Allah.”  
> — Qur’an 8:61

These verses are not marginal. They establish that peace is religiously valid and that Muslims are not given a cause against those who cease hostilities.

## 3. “Jizya” was a pre-modern political tax, not a license for violence

The opponent presents jizya as proof that Islam promotes violence toward non-Muslims. But jizya was not a command to kill non-Muslims. It was a tax within a pre-modern imperial order, tied to protection and exemption from military service. Muslims paid zakat and were subject to military obligations; non-Muslim protected communities paid jizya and were exempted from certain obligations.

That system was not modern liberal equality, and we do not need to pretend it was. But inequality in a pre-modern tax structure is not the same as promoting violence.

Classical Muslim authorities also recognized exemptions from jizya for women, children, monks, the elderly, the poor, and the disabled. Abu Yusuf, the early Hanafi jurist and chief judge, records in *Kitab al-Kharaj* that if the Muslim state could not protect a non-Muslim community, the jizya could be returned. This shows that the tax was understood as part of a protection arrangement, not simply religious humiliation.

More importantly, once non-Muslims were under covenant, harming them was treated as a major sin. The Prophet said:

> “Whoever kills a person under covenant will not smell the fragrance of Paradise.”  
> — Sahih al-Bukhari 3166

And he also said:

> “Whoever wrongs a person under covenant, diminishes his right, burdens him beyond his capacity, or takes something from him without his consent, I will be his opponent on the Day of Resurrection.”  
> — Sunan Abi Dawud 3052

That is not the language of a religion promoting violence toward non-Muslims.

## 4. The hadith about “Islam, jizya, or fighting” is a rule for military commanders, not civilians

The opponent cites Sahih Muslim 1731a. But the context matters. The Prophet is instructing military commanders when they meet enemy forces. The hadith itself begins with rules of restraint:

> “Fight in the name of Allah… Do not act treacherously, do not mutilate, and do not kill children.”  
> — Sahih Muslim 1731a

So even in a wartime setting, the Prophet’s instruction is not “kill non-Muslims.” It is: no treachery, no mutilation, no killing children, and offer terms before battle.

This is law of war, not promotion of violence against non-Muslims as such.

The same point is reinforced by other hadiths. When the Prophet saw that a woman had been killed in battle, he condemned it and said:

> “She was not one who would have fought.”  
> — Sunan Abi Dawud 2669; also supported by Sahih al-Bukhari 3014/3015 and Sahih Muslim 1744 prohibiting the killing of women and children

That reasoning matters. If disbelief itself were the reason for killing, then women, children, monks, farmers, and elderly non-Muslims would be targets. But they are not. Combatancy and aggression are the operative issues.

## 5. “I have been commanded to fight the people” cannot mean all non-Muslims universally

The opponent also mentions the hadith:

> “I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify that there is no god but Allah…”

This hadith cannot be read in isolation as a universal command to fight every non-Muslim, because the Qur’an and Sunnah themselves recognize Jews, Christians, treaty partners, protected persons, and peaceful non-Muslims who are not to be fought.

If “the people” meant every non-Muslim without exception, then Qur’an 9:6 protecting polytheist asylum-seekers, Qur’an 60:8 commanding kindness to peaceful non-Muslims, and the hadith protecting covenanted non-Muslims would all be meaningless. Classical scholars therefore treated such general wording as qualified by other texts.

Islamic interpretation is not done by taking one text and ignoring the rest. The Qur’an itself says:

> “Fight in the way of Allah those who fight you, but do not transgress. Indeed, Allah does not love transgressors.”  
> — Qur’an 2:190

That remains a controlling moral principle: fighting is limited, transgression is forbidden, and aggression is not permitted.

## 6. Classical jurisprudence was not monolithic

The opponent cites *Reliance of the Traveller*, a Shafi‘i manual, as though one medieval legal manual settles the entire question of what Islam “promotes.” But Islamic jurisprudence was diverse.

Some jurists did articulate expansionist doctrines of jihad, particularly in a world of empires where Byzantines, Persians, Crusaders, and others also understood international relations through conquest and tribute. But other jurists emphasized that the legal cause of fighting was hostile aggression, not disbelief itself.

Hanafi jurists, for example, generally placed greater emphasis on combatancy and hostile power rather than mere unbelief. This is reflected in the fact that noncombatants are not to be killed. The prohibition on killing women, children, monks, the elderly, and other noncombatants makes little sense if non-Muslim belief itself is the cause of violence.

Even medieval jurists who accepted offensive jihad did not authorize random violence by ordinary Muslims. Jihad was a state matter, governed by the ruler, treaties, truces, noncombatant immunity, and rules of conduct. That is very different from saying Islam promotes violence toward non-Muslims generally.

## 7. Abrogation claims are overstated

The opponent argues that “later militant verses” abrogated earlier peaceful verses. But this is not a settled fact.

First, Qur’an 9 itself contains limitations: treaty-honoring polytheists are protected in 9:4, and asylum-seeking polytheists are protected in 9:6. So even the so-called “Sword Verse” cannot be read as abolishing all peaceful relations.

Second, Qur’an 60:8 commands kindness and justice toward peaceful non-Muslims. This verse is Medinan and legally significant. It was not simply erased.

Third, the principle “There is no compulsion in religion” remained central in Islamic law. Non-Muslims under Muslim rule were not generally forced to convert; the very existence of jizya and protected communities presupposes that conversion cannot be compelled.

The Qur’an states plainly:

> “There is no compulsion in religion.”  
> — Qur’an 2:256

And Ibn Kathir, a major classical commentator, explains this verse as meaning that no one should be forced to enter Islam because its truth is clear and does not require compulsion.

So the claim that Islam’s peaceful teachings were simply cancelled by later verses is far too simplistic.

## 8. Early Muslim conquests do not prove that Islam promotes violence toward non-Muslims

The opponent points to early Islamic conquests. But historical expansion by Muslim empires proves that Muslim states, like other pre-modern states, engaged in war. It does not prove that Islam promotes violence toward non-Muslims as a religious class.

The fact that large Jewish, Christian, Zoroastrian, Hindu, and other communities survived for centuries under Muslim rule also complicates the opponent’s claim. If Islam’s actual teaching were violence toward non-Muslims as such, these communities would not have endured.

This does not mean Muslim history was perfect. It was not. There were injustices, coercive policies, and episodes of violence. But the debate is not whether Muslims have ever committed violence. The debate is whether Islam itself promotes violence toward non-Muslims. The core sources do not support that sweeping claim.

## Conclusion

The opponent has shown that Islamic law contains doctrines of war. That is true. But a doctrine of war is not the same as promoting violence toward non-Muslims.

The Qur’an commands justice even toward enemies:

> “Do not let the hatred of a people cause you to be unjust. Be just; that is nearer to righteousness.”  
> — Qur’an 5:8

It protects peaceful non-Muslims:

> “Allah does not forbid you from being kind and just toward those who have not fought you…”  
> — Qur’an 60:8

It forbids compulsion in religion:

> “There is no compulsion in religion.”  
> — Qur’an 2:256

It limits fighting to those who fight and forbids transgression:

> “Fight those who fight you, but do not transgress.”  
> — Qur’an 2:190

It commands peace when the enemy inclines to peace:

> “If they incline to peace, then incline to it also.”  
> — Qur’an 8:61

And the Prophet severely warned against harming protected non-Muslims:

> “Whoever kills a person under covenant will not smell the fragrance of Paradise.”  
> — Sahih al-Bukhari 3166

Therefore, the proposition remains false. Islam does not promote violence toward non-Muslims. It permits regulated warfare under specific conditions, as every major civilization has done, but it also commands justice, forbids religious compulsion, protects noncombatants and treaty partners, and praises kindness toward peaceful non-Muslims.

conclusions.for:
Ladies and gentlemen,

In conclusion, my argument has not been that all Muslims are violent, nor that peaceful Muslim interpretations are insincere or impossible. Many Muslims live peacefully with people of other faiths, and Islam undeniably contains verses and traditions emphasizing justice, restraint, mercy, and protection for certain non-Muslims.

But that is not enough to defeat the proposition.

The central question is whether Islam’s foundational texts and classical legal tradition contain authoritative teachings that have promoted, justified, or institutionalized violence and coercive domination toward non-Muslims. On that question, the evidence is clear.

The Qur’an contains passages such as Qur’an 9:5, commanding the fighting of polytheists after the sacred months, and Qur’an 9:29, commanding fighting against Jews and Christians until they pay jizya in a state of submission. These are not merely abstract spiritual metaphors. They were historically understood by many classical jurists as legal foundations for armed jihad and Islamic political supremacy.

The hadith literature reinforces this. Reports such as “I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify…” and the instruction in Sahih Muslim to invite enemies to Islam, then jizya, and then fight if they refuse, establish a framework in which non-Muslim communities could be confronted with conversion, submission, or war.

Classical jurisprudence developed these ideas into a legal doctrine of jihad. Authorities in the major legal schools treated armed struggle against non-Muslim polities not merely as defensive warfare, but as a collective duty connected to the expansion or maintenance of Islamic rule. Manuals such as *Reliance of the Traveller* explicitly describe fighting Jews, Christians, Zoroastrians, and others until they accept Islam or submit through jizya. Scholars such as Majid Khadduri, Rudolph Peters, and David Cook have documented that classical jihad was understood primarily as armed struggle, not simply inner moral effort.

The opposition has rightly cited verses such as “There is no compulsion in religion,” “Fight those who fight you,” and commands to be kind and just toward peaceful non-Muslims. But those verses do not erase the militant texts, nor do they erase the way much of the classical tradition interpreted them. A religion can contain both peaceful teachings and doctrines of sanctioned violence. The presence of one does not cancel the other.

Nor does the protection of dhimmis or covenanted non-Muslims disprove the point. Those protections applied within a system of submission. Non-Muslims were protected after accepting Muslim political authority, paying jizya, and occupying a subordinate legal status. That is not equal coexistence; it is conditional toleration backed by force.

History also reflects this pattern. The early Islamic conquests were not limited to immediate self-defense. Muslim armies expanded across vast non-Muslim territories, and conquered populations were often allowed to retain their faith only under Islamic rule and taxation. This historical reality aligns closely with the doctrines found in scripture, hadith, and classical law.

So the proposition should be understood carefully. Islam does not necessarily command indiscriminate violence against every non-Muslim, and many Muslims today reject militant interpretations. But Islam’s foundational sources and classical jurisprudence have indeed contained and transmitted doctrines that authorize fighting non-Muslims, subjugating them politically, and imposing religiously defined hierarchy.

That is the burden I set out to prove, and the evidence supports it.

Therefore, while acknowledging peaceful interpretations and the peaceful lives of many Muslims, I maintain that the proposition stands: within Islamic scripture and classical legal tradition, there are significant doctrines that have promoted or legitimized violence and coercive domination toward non-Muslims.
conclusions.against:
Ladies and gentlemen,

The proposition before us is that **“Islam promotes violence towards non-Muslims.”** That is a sweeping claim, and throughout this debate I have argued that it is not supported by a fair reading of Islam’s sources.

My opponent has shown that Islamic civilization, like other pre-modern civilizations, developed doctrines of war, conquest, taxation, treaties, and political rule. I do not deny that. But the existence of Islamic laws governing warfare does **not** prove that Islam promotes violence against non-Muslims as a religious class.

The central question is this: **Does Islam command Muslims to attack, harm, or kill non-Muslims simply because they are non-Muslims?** The answer is no.

The Qur’an repeatedly distinguishes between peaceful non-Muslims and hostile aggressors. It says:

> **“Allah does not forbid you from being kind and just toward those who have not fought you because of religion and have not driven you from your homes.”**  
> — Qur’an 60:8

That verse alone seriously undermines the proposition. Islam does not merely tolerate peaceful relations with non-Muslims; it praises kindness and justice toward them.

The Qur’an also states:

> **“There is no compulsion in religion.”**  
> — Qur’an 2:256

If Islam promoted violence toward non-Muslims as such, forced conversion would be central. Instead, the Qur’an rejects religious compulsion.

Where fighting is permitted, it is limited by cause and conduct:

> **“Fight in the way of Allah those who fight you, but do not transgress.”**  
> — Qur’an 2:190

That is not a blank cheque for violence. It is a restriction: fight those who fight you, and even then, do not transgress.

The opponent relied heavily on verses such as Qur’an 9:5 and 9:29. But those verses cannot honestly be read in isolation. Qur’an 9 itself protects treaty-honoring polytheists, commands safe passage for polytheists seeking protection, and explains the cause of fighting as treaty-breaking, expulsion, and aggression. The so-called “Sword Verse” is not a universal command to kill non-Muslims.

Likewise, hadiths about military commanders offering Islam, jizya, or battle are instructions in a wartime setting. They are not commands for ordinary Muslims to commit violence against non-Muslims. In fact, those same military instructions prohibit treachery, mutilation, and the killing of children. Other hadiths prohibit killing women and noncombatants. This shows that combatancy, not mere disbelief, is the relevant issue.

The Prophet Muhammad also gave severe warnings against harming non-Muslims under covenant:

> **“Whoever kills a person under covenant will not smell the fragrance of Paradise.”**  
> — Sahih al-Bukhari 3166

And:

> **“Whoever wrongs a person under covenant… I will be his opponent on the Day of Resurrection.”**  
> — Sunan Abi Dawud 3052

This is not the language of a religion that promotes violence toward non-Muslims. It is the language of moral accountability, protection, and restraint.

Nor can historical Muslim conquests settle the question. Muslim empires, like Christian, Persian, Roman, Mongol, and other empires, fought wars and expanded territory. That proves that Muslims, like others, participated in the politics of their age. It does not prove that Islam itself promotes violence against non-Muslims. Indeed, the survival of large Christian, Jewish, Zoroastrian, Hindu, and other communities under Muslim rule for centuries shows that Islamic rule was not based on extermination or forced conversion.

To be clear, I am not claiming that Muslim history has always been peaceful or just. It has not. No major civilization’s history is free of violence or oppression. But the debate is not whether Muslims have ever committed violence. The debate is whether Islam, as a religion, promotes violence toward non-Muslims. The evidence does not support that claim.

Islam commands justice even toward enemies:

> **“Do not let the hatred of a people cause you to be unjust. Be just; that is nearer to righteousness.”**  
> — Qur’an 5:8

It commands peace when peace is offered:

> **“If they incline to peace, then incline to it also.”**  
> — Qur’an 8:61

It protects religious communities, including churches, synagogues, monasteries, and mosques:

> — Qur’an 22:39–40

And it presents human diversity not as a reason for hatred, but as part of God’s design:

> **“We made you peoples and tribes so that you may know one another.”**  
> — Qur’an 49:13

So my conclusion is simple: **Islam does not promote violence toward non-Muslims.** It permits regulated warfare under specific conditions, especially against aggression, persecution, treachery, and hostile forces. But it also forbids compulsion, prohibits transgression, protects noncombatants and treaty partners, and commands kindness and justice toward peaceful non-Muslims.

The proposition therefore fails. It confuses Islamic laws of war with a general promotion of violence, and it mistakes selective readings for the whole tradition. A fair reading of the Qur’an, the Prophet’s teachings, and Islamic ethics leads to one conclusion: **Islam promotes justice, restraint, and peaceful coexistence — not violence toward non-Muslims.**
